question: In the face of the severe drought ravaging the European Mediterranean basin, the Spanish Government has granted extraordinary drought aid to farmers and reviewed certain environmental requirements1 under the common agricultural policy (CAP). The most recent aid was granted in July 2023 to Catalonia for dryland herbaceous crops.

However, in 2024, water scarcity is even more acute, and Catalonia is entering its 38th month of continued drought. As a result, restrictions have been imposed and water use by farmers has been cut by between 50%80%, affecting more than 4 000 hectares of crops2. ‘Many farmers who feared losing crop yields to fires, droughts and floods were already making a transition to more sustainable practices’3.
Aid from Member States is not adequate to tackle the effects of the drought. A paradigm shift is needed to ensure the future of European agriculture amid the impacts of climate change. 1.
Will the Commission propose measures to improve and streamline long-term water resilience across the Union in order to mitigate the consequences of severe droughts that farmers are facing?

Will the next CAP reform include a specific chapter on European and national measures to mitigate and adapt to extreme consequences of global warming, such as the current longest drought ever recorded in southern Europe?
answer: 1. The Commission is aware of the severe drought situation in Catalonia and the considerable production losses in the agricultural sector. As outlined in the recently published Communication on managing climate risks (4), climate change is projected to further aggravate water scarcity and the frequency, intensity and length of drought episodes (5), especially in Southern Europe.

The Commission is taking stock of water issues comprehensively, building upon the findings of the ongoing assessments of River Basin and Flood Risk Management Plans and on that basis will consider the need for action. It is critical for the EU agricultural sector to adapt to climate change and become more water resilient.

The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) (6) offers a wide range of tools to support the sector’s transition to increased water resilience. This includes support for agricultural practices increasing soil health and water retention capacity, support for diversification of production, and more drought resistant/ less water intensive crops or varieties.

Investments in smart water management and the use of recycled water (7) can also be financed, along with natural water retention measures based on resilient (freshwater) ecosystems. Support is also available for risk and crisis management, including short-term emergency measures.

The Spanish authorities may also grant further support to farmers to compensate the damage caused by severe drought in line with the EU state aid rules (8). 2. There is a need for the CAP post-2027 to support farmers in addressing severe droughts and other necessary adaptations to changing climate.
The Commission will present a legislative proposal for the post-2027 CAP, including the modalities of such support, in due time.
